features.note: From each project's public page on 9 Nov 2026 (ltspice-mcp: PyPI page; mcp-spice: Glama listing; spicebridge: search listing only, its page did not load). Not run here: installing third-party packages was blocked in this sandbox. Treat 'not stated' as unknown, not as missing.

headline: All three ways met every spec at nominal on all three circuits. For simple, well-known circuits a strong model with no tools already gets the textbook answer. SpiceMCP did not beat it on pass rate.

Yield was a tie on the RC filter and the buck, and SpiceMCP lost on the amplifier (66.5% vs 67.5% model alone vs 89% model + simulator). The 89% came from a 1.01 kΩ resistor, a value you cannot buy; with 1.00 kΩ it is 67.5%. A centred buyable pair (10.2 kΩ / 1.13 kΩ) reaches 91%, so SpiceMCP left 25 points on the table.

The RC filter caps out near 40% for everyone: ±2% cutoff with 5% capacitors is not buildable reliably. SpiceMCP was the only arm that said so and named the fix (tighter capacitor); the plain model also flagged it in words.

Where SpiceMCP clearly wins is what you get back: a measured yield, a parts list in buyable values, the ratings to buy each part at, a drawn schematic and a report. The other arms return a netlist and a claim.

Where it loses: slowest (14 min for the buck, mostly the 90-run yield check) and about 35% more billed tokens than a model driving a raw simulator. Its smallest-parts goal also leaves thinner margins (buck ripple up to 44 of 50 mV vs 5 mV with bigger capacitors).
honest: This benchmark does not show that SpiceMCP designs better circuits than a strong model. On these three it designs about the same circuits.

Its value here is verification and paperwork: it measured yield over 30 to 200 boards at three temperatures and a ±5% supply, while the model-alone arm said 'meets spec' without checking and was right only at nominal.

The model + raw simulator arm checked corners by itself, but hit a simulator convergence failure it could not fix, used a non-standard resistor, and spent 37 runs and 3 minutes doing what one SpiceMCP call does.
The model-alone buck used an ideal switch, which is not a part you can buy and skips the gate drive. It still passed, so the checker does not punish idealisations; a stricter benchmark should.
The baselines were handed SpiceMCP's own working op-amp and comparator models. That removes the hardest part of the buck for them, so the buck result flatters the baselines.
The model used for the baselines is a strong one. SpiceMCP is meant to help weaker models; that case is untested here and is where the gap should be largest.
fixes: finish_design should centre ratios, not just snap each value: search standard-value pairs for the one closest to the middle of the limits. On the amplifier that lifts yield from 66.5% to 91%.

Do not shrink parts to the edge by default: the 'smallest capacitor / inductor' goals left the buck at 44 mV worst-case ripple against a 50 mV limit. Aim for the middle of the limit, or give the user the size-vs-margin choice.
Make long finishes cheaper to wait for: 13 identical polling calls cost about 70k billed tokens on the buck. Return an estimated finish time and tell the model to wait that long.
Say 'not buildable at this tolerance' up front: when the spec window is narrower than the part tolerance (RC ±2% with 5% capacitors), say so before optimising.
limits: Three circuits, one run each; model arms are not repeated, so luck is not averaged out.

Simulation only (ngspice 42). The buck ripple needs a 2 ns time step to be honest: at 20 ns SpiceMCP's buck reads 180 mV. The raw-simulator buck only runs at 20 ns or 5 ns, so its ripple number is less certain.
Buck yield is 30 boards per arm (90 runs at three temperatures): 30/30 means at least 90% with 95% confidence. RC and amplifier use 200 boards.
Tokens are counted with an older public tokenizer and exclude the tool harness's own system prompt, which is the same for every arm.
